claim: I-BET151 is a small-molecule inhibitor of a family of bromodomain-containing transcriptional regulators.
source: We report that a short treatment with I-BET151, a small-molecule inhibitor of a family of bromodomain-containing transcriptional regulators, irreversibly suppressed development of type-1 diabetes in NOD mice.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a definition of I-BET151.

claim: A short treatment with I-BET151 irreversibly suppressed development of type-1 diabetes in NOD mice.
source: We report that a short treatment with I-BET151, a small-molecule inhibitor of a family of bromodomain-containing transcriptional regulators, irreversibly suppressed development of type-1 diabetes in NOD mice.
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: I-BET151 could prevent or clear insulitis in NOD mice.
source: The inhibitor could prevent or clear insulitis, but had minimal influence on the transcriptomes of infiltrating and circulating T cells.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: I-BET151 had minimal influence on the transcriptomes of infiltrating and circulating T cells.
source: The inhibitor could prevent or clear insulitis, but had minimal influence on the transcriptomes of infiltrating and circulating T cells.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: I-BET151 induced pancreatic macrophages to adopt an anti-inflammatory phenotype.
source: Rather, it induced pancreatic macrophages to adopt an anti-inflammatory phenotype, impacting the NF-κB pathway in particular.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: I-BET151 impacts the NF-κB pathway in pancreatic macrophages.
source: Rather, it induced pancreatic macrophages to adopt an anti-inflammatory phenotype, impacting the NF-κB pathway in particular.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: I-BET151 elicited regeneration of islet β-cells.
source: I-BET151 also elicited regeneration of islet β-cells, inducing proliferation and expression of genes encoding transcription factors key to β-cell differentiation/function.
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 6D and 6G, and transcriptome data in Figure 6A-B.

claim: I-BET151 induced proliferation of β-cells.
source: I-BET151 also elicited regeneration of islet β-cells, inducing proliferation and expression of genes encoding transcription factors key to β-cell differentiation/function.
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 6D and 6G.

claim: I-BET151 induced expression of genes encoding transcription factors key to β-cell differentiation/function.
source: I-BET151 also elicited regeneration of islet β-cells, inducing proliferation and expression of genes encoding transcription factors key to β-cell differentiation/function.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The effect of I-BET151 on β cells did not require T cell infiltration of the islets.
source: The effect on β cells did not require T cell infiltration of the islets.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in NOD.Rag−/− mice shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: Acetylation of lysine residues on histones and non-histone proteins is an important epigenetic modification of chromatin.
source: Acetylation of lysine residues on histones and non-histone proteins is an important epigenetic modification of chromatin (Kouzarides, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kouzarides, 2000.

claim: Chromatin acetylation impacts multiple fundamental cellular processes.
source: Chromatin acetylation impacts multiple fundamental cellular processes, and its dysregulation has been linked to a variety of disease states, notably various cancers (Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012.

claim: Dysregulation of chromatin acetylation has been linked to various cancers.
source: Chromatin acetylation impacts multiple fundamental cellular processes, and its dysregulation has been linked to a variety of disease states, notably various cancers (Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dawson and Kouzarides, 2012.

claim: BRDs are domains of approximately 110 amino-acids that recognize acetylation marks on histones.
source: BRDs, conserved from yeast to humans, are domains of approximately 110 amino-acids that recognize acetylation marks on histones (primarily H3 and H4) and certain non-histone proteins (e.g., the transcription factor, NF-κB), and serve as scaffolds for the assembly of multi-protein complexes that regulate transcription (Dawson et al., 2011; Prinjha et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dawson et al., 2011 and Prinjha et al., 2012.

claim: BRDs recognize acetylation marks on certain non-histone proteins such as NF-κB.
source: BRDs, conserved from yeast to humans, are domains of approximately 110 amino-acids that recognize acetylation marks on histones (primarily H3 and H4) and certain non-histone proteins (e.g., the transcription factor, NF-κB), and serve as scaffolds for the assembly of multi-protein complexes that regulate transcription (Dawson et al., 2011; Prinjha et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dawson et al., 2011 and Prinjha et al., 2012.

claim: BRDs serve as scaffolds for the assembly of multi-protein complexes that regulate transcription.
source: BRDs, conserved from yeast to humans, are domains of approximately 110 amino-acids that recognize acetylation marks on histones (primarily H3 and H4) and certain non-histone proteins (e.g., the transcription factor, NF-κB), and serve as scaffolds for the assembly of multi-protein complexes that regulate transcription (Dawson et al., 2011; Prinjha et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dawson et al., 2011 and Prinjha et al., 2012.

claim: The BET subfamily of BRD-containing proteins includes BRDs 2, 3, 4 and T.
source: The BET subfamily of BRD-containing proteins (BRDs 2, 3, 4 and T) is distinguished as having tandem bromodomains followed by an 'extra-terminal' domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the BET protein family.

claim: The BET subfamily is distinguished as having tandem bromodomains followed by an 'extra-terminal' domain.
source: The BET subfamily of BRD-containing proteins (BRDs 2, 3, 4 and T) is distinguished as having tandem bromodomains followed by an 'extra-terminal' domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the BET protein family structure.

claim: Brd4 is critical for 'bookmarking' transcribed loci post-mitotically.
source: One of its members, Brd4, is critical for both 'bookmarking' transcribed loci post-mitotically (Zhao et al., 2011) and surmounting RNA polymerase pausing downstream of transcription initiation (Jang et al., 2005; Hargreaves et al., 2009; Anand et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2011.

claim: Brd4 is critical for surmounting RNA polymerase pausing downstream of transcription initiation.
source: One of its members, Brd4, is critical for both 'bookmarking' transcribed loci post-mitotically (Zhao et al., 2011) and surmounting RNA polymerase pausing downstream of transcription initiation (Jang et al., 2005; Hargreaves et al., 2009; Anand et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jang et al., 2005; Hargreaves et al., 2009; Anand et al., 2013; Patel et al., 2013.

claim: Small-molecule inhibitors of BET proteins (JQ1 and I-BET) were found to be effective inhibitors of multiple types of mouse tumors.
source: Recently, small-molecule inhibitors of BET proteins, for example, JQ1 and I-BET, were found to be effective inhibitors of multiple types of mouse tumors, including a NUT midline carcinoma, leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma (Filippakopoulos et al., 2010; Dawson et al., 2011; Delmore et al., 2011; Zuber et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Filippakopoulos et al., 2010; Dawson et al., 2011; Delmore et al., 2011; Zuber et al., 2011.

claim: BET-protein inhibitors could prevent or reverse endotoxic shock induced by systemic injection of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
source: In addition, BET-protein inhibitors could prevent or reverse endotoxic shock induced by systemic injection of bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (Nicodeme et al., 2010; Seal et al., 2012; Belkina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nicodeme et al., 2010; Seal et al., 2012; Belkina et al., 2013.

claim: The primary cellular focus of BET-protein inhibitor action in endotoxic shock was macrophages.
source: The primary cellular focus of action was macrophages, and genes induced by the transcription factor NF-κB were key molecular targets (Nicodeme et al., 2010; Belkina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nicodeme et al., 2010; Belkina et al., 2013.

claim: Genes induced by the transcription factor NF-κB were key molecular targets of BET-protein inhibitors in endotoxic shock.
source: The primary cellular focus of action was macrophages, and genes induced by the transcription factor NF-κB were key molecular targets (Nicodeme et al., 2010; Belkina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nicodeme et al., 2010; Belkina et al., 2013.

claim: Type-1 diabetes is hallmarked by specific destruction of the insulin-producing β cells of the pancreatic islets.
source: We wondered how they might impact type-1 diabetes (T1D), hallmarked by specific destruction of the insulin-producing β cells of the pancreatic islets (Bluestone et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bluestone et al., 2010.

claim: NOD mice are the 'gold standard' T1D model.
source: NOD mice, the 'gold standard' T1D model (Anderson and Bluestone, 2005), spontaneously and universally develop insulitis at 4–6 weeks of age, while overt diabetes manifests in a subset of individuals beginning from 12–15 weeks, depending on the particular colony.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Anderson and Bluestone, 2005.

claim: NOD mice spontaneously and universally develop insulitis at 4–6 weeks of age.
source: NOD mice, the 'gold standard' T1D model (Anderson and Bluestone, 2005), spontaneously and universally develop insulitis at 4–6 weeks of age, while overt diabetes manifests in a subset of individuals beginning from 12–15 weeks, depending on the particular colony.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Anderson and Bluestone, 2005.

claim: Overt diabetes manifests in a subset of NOD mice beginning from 12–15 weeks, depending on the particular colony.
source: NOD mice, the 'gold standard' T1D model (Anderson and Bluestone, 2005), spontaneously and universally develop insulitis at 4–6 weeks of age, while overt diabetes manifests in a subset of individuals beginning from 12–15 weeks, depending on the particular colony.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Anderson and Bluestone, 2005.

claim: NOD diabetes is primarily a T-cell-mediated disease.
source: NOD diabetes is primarily a T-cell-mediated disease, but other immune cells—such as B cells, natural killer cells, macrophages (MFs) and dendritic cells (DCs)—also play significant roles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NOD diabetes pathogenesis.

claim: Other immune cells such as B cells, natural killer cells, macrophages and dendritic cells also play significant roles in NOD diabetes.
source: NOD diabetes is primarily a T-cell-mediated disease, but other immune cells—such as B cells, natural killer cells, macrophages (MFs) and dendritic cells (DCs)—also play significant roles.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NOD diabetes pathogenesis.

claim: I-BET151 prevented diabetes development in NOD mice with incipient insulitis (treated from 3-5 weeks of age).
source: I-BET151 prevented diabetes development, no matter whether the treated cohort had incipient (Figure 1A) or established (Figure 1B) insulitis.
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: I-BET151 prevented diabetes development in NOD mice with established insulitis (treated from 12-14 weeks of age).
source: I-BET151 prevented diabetes development, no matter whether the treated cohort had incipient (Figure 1A) or established (Figure 1B) insulitis.
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Long-term protection from diabetes afforded by a 2-week treatment of pre-diabetic mice was only rarely observed with recent-onset diabetic animals.
source: However, the long-term protection afforded by a 2-week treatment of pre-diabetic mice was only rarely observed with recent-onset diabetic animals.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Normoglycemia was significantly prolonged in recent-onset diabetic mice treated for 2 weeks with I-BET151.
source: Normoglycemia was significantly prolonged in mice treated for 2 weeks with I-BET151; but, upon drug removal, hyperglycemia rapidly ensued in most animals (Figure 1C, lower and right panels).
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Upon I-BET151 removal, hyperglycemia rapidly ensued in most recent-onset diabetic animals.
source: Normoglycemia was significantly prolonged in mice treated for 2 weeks with I-BET151; but, upon drug removal, hyperglycemia rapidly ensued in most animals (Figure 1C, lower and right panels).
evidence: This is supported by blood glucose data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The lack of disease reversal in recent-onset diabetic mice suggests that β-cell destruction had proceeded to the point that dampening the autoinflammatory attack was not enough to stem hyperglycemia.
source: The lack of disease reversal under these conditions suggests that β-cell destruction had proceeded to the point that dampening the autoinflammatory attack was not enough to stem hyperglycemia.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from Figure 1C.

claim: Drug treatment with I-BET151 prevented effective installation of insulitis in young NOD mice (treated from 3-5 weeks).
source: Drug treatment prevented effective installation of insulitis in the young mice (Figure 1D) and reversed established insulitis in the older animals (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: I-BET151 treatment reversed established insulitis in older NOD mice (treated from 12-14 weeks).
source: Drug treatment prevented effective installation of insulitis in the young mice (Figure 1D) and reversed established insulitis in the older animals (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fewer total leukocytes (CD45+ cells) were found in the pancreas of mice administered I-BET151 from 12–14 weeks of age compared to vehicle-only controls.
source: Consistent with the histological results, fewer total leukocytes (CD45+ cells) were found in the pancreas, but not the spleen, of mice administered I-BET151 from 12–14 weeks of age, vis a vis vehicle-only controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: I-BET151 treatment did not affect total leukocyte numbers in the spleen.
source: Consistent with the histological results, fewer total leukocytes (CD45+ cells) were found in the pancreas, but not the spleen, of mice administered I-BET151 from 12–14 weeks of age, vis a vis vehicle-only controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The fractional representation of major lymphoid and myeloid subsets within the bulk CD45+ compartment appeared to be unaltered in drug- vs vehicle-treated individuals.
source: The drop in pancreas-infiltrating cells in animals treated with the inhibitor was equally true of all populations examined (encompassing the major lymphoid and myeloid subsets) as their fractional representation within the bulk CD45+ compartment appeared to be unaltered in drug- vs vehicle-treated individuals (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The 2-week I-BET151 treatment protocol had surprisingly little impact on the transcriptome of CD4+ T cells isolated from the infiltrated pancreas, draining pancreatic lymph nodes, and control inguinal lymph nodes.
source: Microarray analysis of gene expression revealed surprisingly little impact of the 2-week treatment protocol on any of these populations, similar to what was observed when comparing randomly shuffled datasets (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Minimal, background-level, differences were observed in the gene-expression profiles of pancreas-infiltrating CD4+ T cells at 12, 24 or 48 hr after a single administration of I-BET151.
source: Again, minimal, background-level, differences were observed in the gene-expression profiles of drug- and vehicle-treated mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Signature analysis failed to reveal statistically significant skewing of Th1, Th2, Th17 or Treg gene-expression signatures within the transcriptomes of pancreatic CD4+ T cells from mice administered I-BET151 vs vehicle.
source: Signature analysis, wherein we superimposed existing Th1, Th2, Th17 or Treg gene-expression signatures on p-value vs fold-change (FC) volcano plots, failed to reveal statistically significant skewing within the transcriptomes of pancreatic CD4+ T cells from mice administered I-BET151 vs vehicle using either the 2-week or short-term protocols, with the possible exception of a slightly weaker Treg down-signature in I-BET151-treated animals (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by signature analysis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There were no differences in the fraction of Tregs in the pancreatic CD4+ T cell compartment between I-BET151- and vehicle-treated mice.
source: Yet, we found no differences in the fraction of Tregs in the pancreatic CD4+ T cell compartment, their Foxp3 expression levels or their display of CD25 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There were no differences in Foxp3 expression levels or CD25 display by Tregs between I-BET151- and vehicle-treated mice.
source: Yet, we found no differences in the fraction of Tregs in the pancreatic CD4+ T cell compartment, their Foxp3 expression levels or their display of CD25 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There were no differences in the Th17 population (either the fraction of CD4+ cells expressing IL-17A or its expression level) between I-BET151- and vehicle-treated mice.
source: Nor, in contrast to a recent report on antigen + adjuvant induced autoimmune diseases (Mele et al., 2013), could we demonstrate differences in the Th17 population—either the fraction of CD4+ cells expressing IL-17A or its expression level (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The 2-week and short-term I-BET151 treatment protocols both resulted in sets of over- and under-represented transcripts in the bulk CD45+ cell population.
source: The 2-week and short-term treatment protocols both resulted in sets of over- and under-represented transcripts (Figure 3A,B and Supplementary files 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The set of decreased transcripts was evident sooner than the set of increased transcripts—the former troughing already at 12 hr, the latter still rising at 48 hr.
source: Interestingly, the set of decreased transcripts was evident sooner than the set of increased transcripts—the former troughing already at 12 hr, the latter still rising at 48 hr (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by time-course microarray data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The over-represented transcripts in CD45+ cells were indicative of myeloid-lineage cells, in particular tissue-resident macrophages.
source: Taking advantage of data-sets from the Immunological Genome Project (ImmGen; www.immgen.org), which has profiled gene expression for over 200 immunocyte populations, we found the over-represented transcripts to be indicative of myeloid-lineage cells, in particular tissue-resident MFs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ImmGen analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gene-set enrichment analysis highlighted transcriptional programs characteristic of macrophages, with the highest enrichment values for the eicosanoid, relevant nuclear receptor and complement pathways.
source: Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) also highlighted transcriptional programs characteristic of MFs, the highest enrichment values being obtained for the eicosanoid, relevant nuclear receptor and complement pathways (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The eicosanoid, nuclear receptor and complement pathways have been demonstrated to play a role in the resolution of inflammation.
source: All three of these pathways have been demonstrated to play a role in the resolution of inflammation, through multiple mechanisms, including the production of anti-inflammatory mediators and suppression of T cell responses (Bensinger and Tontonoz, 2008; Ricklin et al., 2010; Serhan, 2011; Lone and Tasken, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bensinger and Tontonoz, 2008; Ricklin et al., 2010; Serhan, 2011; Lone and Tasken, 2013.

claim: Both 2-week and short-term treatment of NOD mice with I-BET151 had a dichotomous effect on the NF-κB target genes expressed by pancreatic leukocytes.
source: Interestingly, both 2-week and short-term treatment of NOD mice with I-BET151 had a dichotomous effect on the NF-κB target genes expressed by pancreatic leukocytes (Figure 4A, upper left panels, and Supplementary file 3; target genes extracted from [Gilmore, 2006]).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Pro-inflammatory genes, particularly those encoding proteins in the TNFα-induced canonical NF-κB activation pathway, were under-represented after I-BET151 treatment.
source: Pathway analysis using Ingenuity showed that, amongst these NF-κB targets, pro-inflammatory genes, particularly those encoding proteins in the tumor necrosis factor (TNF)α-induced canonical NF-κB activation pathway, were under-represented; while anti-inflammatory loci, notably those specifying molecules implicated in signaling by nuclear receptor family members, that is, the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) and liver-X-receptor (LXR) families, were over-represented subsequent to I-BET151 treatment (Figure 4A, upper right).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Anti-inflammatory loci, notably those specifying molecules implicated in signaling by PPAR and LXR families, were over-represented subsequent to I-BET151 treatment.
source: Pathway analysis using Ingenuity showed that, amongst these NF-κB targets, pro-inflammatory genes, particularly those encoding proteins in the tumor necrosis factor (TNF)α-induced canonical NF-κB activation pathway, were under-represented; while anti-inflammatory loci, notably those specifying molecules implicated in signaling by nuclear receptor family members, that is, the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) and liver-X-receptor (LXR) families, were over-represented subsequent to I-BET151 treatment (Figure 4A, upper right).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The TNF-induced NF-κB activation pathway was down-regulated by I-BET151 treatment.
source: These findings were confirmed by examining expression of pathway signature genes derived from the Molecular Signatures Database (www.broadinstitute.org/gsea/msigdb): again the TNF-induced NF-κB activation pathway was down-regulated and the two nuclear receptor pathways up-regulated (Figure 4A, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by signature gene expression data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The PPAR and LXR pathways were up-regulated by I-BET151 treatment.
source: These findings were confirmed by examining expression of pathway signature genes derived from the Molecular Signatures Database (www.broadinstitute.org/gsea/msigdb): again the TNF-induced NF-κB activation pathway was down-regulated and the two nuclear receptor pathways up-regulated (Figure 4A, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by signature gene expression data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There were no effects of I-BET151 on CD45+ cells isolated from the spleen or lymph nodes.
source: There were no such effects on CD45+ cells isolated from the spleen or lymph nodes of the same mice.
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from the transcriptome analysis.

claim: When the sets of genes over- or under-represented in the CD45+ population of I-BET151-treated mice were superimposed on a volcano plot of transcripts from CD45+ cells of animals given BAY 11–7082 vs vehicle, there was an impressive correspondence, particularly for the enriched transcripts.
source: When the sets of genes over- or under-represented in the CD45+ population of I-BET151-treated mice (drawn from Figure 3A,B) were superimposed on a volcano plot of transcripts from CD45+ cells of animals given BAY 11–7082 vs vehicle, there was an impressive correspondence, particularly for the enriched transcripts (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative transcriptome data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Some genes modulated by the BET-protein inhibitor were not affected by the NF-κB inhibitor and vice versa.
source: The match was not perfect, however, as some genes modulated by the BET-protein inhibitor were not affected by the NF-κB inhibitor and vice versa (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative transcriptome data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: BAY 11–7082, even a single dose, could substantially clear NOD insulitis.
source: Perhaps not surprisingly, then, BAY 11–7082, even a single dose, could substantially clear NOD insulitis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The CD11b+ population from the pancreas of vehicle-treated mice was capable of repressing T cell proliferation.
source: The CD11b+ population from the pancreas of vehicle-treated mice was capable of repressing T cell proliferation, but the corresponding population from mice administered I-BET151 exhibited significantly more potent suppressive activity.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro suppression assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The CD11b+ population from the pancreas of mice administered I-BET151 exhibited significantly more potent suppressive activity on T cell proliferation than the corresponding population from vehicle-treated mice.
source: The CD11b+ population from the pancreas of vehicle-treated mice was capable of repressing T cell proliferation, but the corresponding population from mice administered I-BET151 exhibited significantly more potent suppressive activity.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro suppression assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Co-cultured CD11c+ cells did not appear to affect T cell proliferation whether isolated from control- or drug-treated mice.
source: Co-cultured CD11c+ cells did not appear to affect T cell proliferation whether isolated from control- or drug-treated mice.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro suppression assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Treg cells isolated from I-BET151-treated and vehicle-treated mice were equally able to inhibit T cell proliferation.
source: Treg cells isolated from the two types of mice were equally able to inhibit T cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro suppression assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: I-BET151 greatly dampened the typical macrophage response to LPS in human CD14+ cells.
source: A rank-order FC plot showed that the inhibitor greatly dampened the typical MF response to LPS (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data from human macrophages shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Most (32/43) of the NF-κB target genes inhibited in murine CD45+ cells were also suppressed in human macrophages by I-BET151.
source: Focusing on the NF-κB pathway: most (32/43) of the target genes inhibited in murine CD45+ cells were also suppressed in human MFs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative gene expression data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was suppression of secondary, over primary, LPS-response genes by I-BET151 in human macrophages.
source: In particular, there was suppression of secondary, over primary, LPS-response genes (Figure 5C), as was previously reported for BET inhibitor treatment of mouse bone-marrow-derived MFs (Nicodeme et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5C and a citation to Nicodeme et al., 2010.

claim: A set of about 300 transcripts was over-represented >twofold in β cells from NOD mice treated with I-BET151 compared to vehicle.
source: A set of about 300 transcripts was over-represented >twofold in mice given the inhibitor; and about 10-fold fewer were under-represented >twofold (FDR < 5%) (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: About 10-fold fewer transcripts were under-represented >twofold in β cells from NOD mice treated with I-BET151 compared to vehicle.
source: A set of about 300 transcripts was over-represented >twofold in mice given the inhibitor; and about 10-fold fewer were under-represented >twofold (FDR < 5%) (Figure 6A and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The subset of genes whose expression was increased most by I-BET151 in β cells encoded multiple members of the regenerating islet-derived (Reg) protein family.
source: The subset of genes whose expression was increased most by the inhibitor encoded multiple members of the regenerating islet-derived (Reg) protein family, originally identified for their involvement in pancreas regeneration (Figure 6B, in red) (Unno et al., 1992; Huszarik et al., 2010); several transcription factors (TFs) important for regeneration of β-cells (in green) (Pagliuca and Melton, 2013; Shih et al., 2013); and a number of proteins known to enhance insulin production (in blue) (Hirayama et al., 1999; Dai et al., 2006; Winzell and Ahren, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6B and citations to Unno et al., 1992; Huszarik et al., 2010.

claim: The subset of genes whose expression was increased most by I-BET151 in β cells encoded several transcription factors important for regeneration of β-cells.
source: The subset of genes whose expression was increased most by the inhibitor encoded multiple members of the regenerating islet-derived (Reg) protein family, originally identified for their involvement in pancreas regeneration (Figure 6B, in red) (Unno et al., 1992; Huszarik et al., 2010); several transcription factors (TFs) important for regeneration of β-cells (in green) (Pagliuca and Melton, 2013; Shih et al., 2013); and a number of proteins known to enhance insulin production (in blue) (Hirayama et al., 1999; Dai et al., 2006; Winzell and Ahren, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6B and citations to Pagliuca and Melton, 2013; Shih et al., 2013.

claim: The subset of genes whose expression was increased most by I-BET151 in β cells encoded a number of proteins known to enhance insulin production.
source: The subset of genes whose expression was increased most by the inhibitor encoded multiple members of the regenerating islet-derived (Reg) protein family, originally identified for their involvement in pancreas regeneration (Figure 6B, in red) (Unno et al., 1992; Huszarik et al., 2010); several transcription factors (TFs) important for regeneration of β-cells (in green) (Pagliuca and Melton, 2013; Shih et al., 2013); and a number of proteins known to enhance insulin production (in blue) (Hirayama et al., 1999; Dai et al., 2006; Winzell and Ahren, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6B and citations to Hirayama et al., 1999; Dai et al., 2006; Winzell and Ahren, 2007.

claim: The most highly induced subset of genes in β cells also included a number of loci usually associated with neural function.
source: Interestingly, the most highly induced subset of genes also included a number of loci usually associated with neural function, encoding, for example, survival factors (Cntfr, Tox3) or promoters of synaptic development or function (Snap25, Lrrtm2, Lgi1).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The top signaling pathways to emerge via GSEA in β cells were the IGF-1, IGF/mTOR, PDGF and insulin-secretion pathways.
source: The top signaling pathways to emerge via GSEA were the IGF-1, IGF/mTOR, PDGF and insulin-secretion pathways (although, due to the relatively small number of genes involved, statistical significance was not reached).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of β cell transcriptome data.

claim: Both the number and fraction of EdU+ β cells were significantly increased in I-BET151-treated mice.
source: Both the number and fraction of EdU+ β cells were significantly increased in I-BET151-treated mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Most of the β-cell transcripts over-represented >twofold by treatment of standard NOD mice with I-BET151 were also increased in inhibitor-injected NOD mice lacking T and B cells.
source: Transcriptional analysis revealed that most of the β-cell transcripts over-represented >twofold by treatment of standard NOD mice with I-BET151 were also increased in inhibitor-injected NOD mice lacking T and B cells, and thereby devoid of insulitis (Figure 6E; and the transcripts highlighted in panel 6B are precisely positioned in panel 6F).
evidence: This is supported by comparative transcriptome data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: There was a clear induction of β-cell proliferation in the absence of insulitis in NOD.Rag−/− mice.
source: In addition, there was a clear induction of β-cell proliferation in the absence of insulitis (Figure 6, panel G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: No consistent differences were observed when purified islets from 12-week-old NOD mice were cultured for 24 hr in the presence of I-BET151 or just vehicle.
source: We attempted to further evaluate the cell autonomy of I-BET151's effects on β cells by purifying islets from 12-week-old NOD mice and culturing them for 24 hr in the presence of inhibitor or just vehicle. No consistent differences were observed under the two culture conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from in vitro culture experiments.

claim: A similar experiment using commercially available human islets failed to show a repeatable difference when they were cultured in the presence and absence of I-BET151.
source: Not surprisingly, then, a similar experiment using commercially available human islets failed to show a repeatable difference when they were cultured in the presence and absence of I-BET151.
evidence: This is stated as a negative result from in vitro culture experiments with human islets.

claim: The islet isolation/culture conditions removed or destroyed a critical factor necessary for I-BET151's effects on β cells.
source: Clearly, the islet isolation/culture conditions removed or destroyed a critical factor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the negative results from in vitro culture experiments.

claim: Treatment of NOD mice with I-BET151 for a mere 2 weeks prevented the development of NOD diabetes life-long.
source: The studies presented here showed that treatment of NOD mice with the epigenetic modifier, I-BET151, for a mere 2 weeks prevented the development of NOD diabetes life-long.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding supported by data in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: I-BET151 was able to inhibit impending insulitis as well as clear existing islet infiltration.
source: I-BET151 was able to inhibit impending insulitis as well as clear existing islet infiltration.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: The striking effect of I-BET151 on T1D development in NOD mice seems to reflect the fortunate concurrence of a complex, though inter-related, set of diabetes-protective processes.
source: In brief, the striking effect of I-BET151 on T1D development in NOD mice seems to reflect the fortunate concurrence of a complex, though inter-related, set of diabetes-protective processes.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the mechanistic findings.

claim: Macrophages were shown long ago to be an early participant in islet infiltration.
source: They were shown long ago to be an early participant in islet infiltration (Jansen et al., 1994), and to play a critical effector role in diabetes pathogenesis, attributed primarily to the production of inflammatory cytokines and other mediators, such as iNOS (Hutchings et al., 1990; Jun et al., 1999a, 1999b; Calderon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jansen et al., 1994.

claim: Macrophages play a critical effector role in diabetes pathogenesis, attributed primarily to the production of inflammatory cytokines and other mediators, such as iNOS.
source: They were shown long ago to be an early participant in islet infiltration (Jansen et al., 1994), and to play a critical effector role in diabetes pathogenesis, attributed primarily to the production of inflammatory cytokines and other mediators, such as iNOS (Hutchings et al., 1990; Jun et al., 1999a, 1999b; Calderon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hutchings et al., 1990; Jun et al., 1999a, 1999b; Calderon et al., 2006.

claim: The frequency of a small subset of pancreatic macrophages expressing CRIg at 6–10 weeks of age determined whether or not NOD diabetes would develop months later.
source: For example, the frequency of a small subset of pancreatic MFs expressing the complement receptor for immunoglobulin (a.k.a. CRIg) at 6–10 weeks of age determined whether or not NOD diabetes would develop months later (Fu et al., 2012b), and transfer of in-vitro-differentiated M2, but not M1, MFs protected NOD mice from disease development (Parsa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fu et al., 2012b.

claim: Transfer of in-vitro-differentiated M2, but not M1, macrophages protected NOD mice from disease development.
source: For example, the frequency of a small subset of pancreatic MFs expressing the complement receptor for immunoglobulin (a.k.a. CRIg) at 6–10 weeks of age determined whether or not NOD diabetes would develop months later (Fu et al., 2012b), and transfer of in-vitro-differentiated M2, but not M1, MFs protected NOD mice from disease development (Parsa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Parsa et al., 2012.

claim: Macrophages seem to be playing the driving role in I-BET151's long-term immunologic impact on T1D.
source: One normally thinks of immunological tolerance as being the purview of T and B cells, but MFs seem to be playing the driving role in I-BET151's long-term immunologic impact on T1D.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: BET-protein inhibition skewed the phenotype of pancreatic macrophages towards an anti-inflammatory phenotype.
source: BET-protein inhibition skewed the phenotype of pancreatic MFs towards an anti-inflammatory phenotype, whether this be at the population level through differential influx, efflux or death, or at the level of individual cells owing to changes in transcriptional programs.
evidence: This is an interpretive summary of the findings supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The 're-educated' macrophages appeared to be more potent at inhibiting T cell proliferation.
source: The 're-educated' macrophages appeared to be more potent at inhibiting T cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro suppression assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: It is possible that macrophages play some role in the I-BET151 influences on β-cell regeneration.
source: In addition, it is possible that MFs play some role in the I-BET151 influences on β-cell regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: The findings on Rag1-deficient mice ruled out the need for adaptive immune cells in the islet infiltrate for I-BET151's induction of β-cell proliferation.
source: The findings on Rag1-deficient mice ruled out the need for adaptive immune cells in the islet infiltrate for I-BET151's induction of β-cell proliferation, but MFs are not thought to be compromised in this strain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from Figure 6E-G.

claim: The lack of a consistent I-BET151 effect on cultured mouse and human islets might result from a dearth of macrophages under the isolation and incubation conditions.
source: Relatedly, the lack of a consistent I-BET151 effect on cultured mouse and human islets might result from a dearth of MFs under our isolation and incubation conditions (e.g., [Li et al., 2009]).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the negative in vitro results, supported by a citation to Li et al., 2009.

claim: Several recent publications have highlighted a role for macrophages, particularly M2 cells, in promoting regeneration of β cells in diverse experimental settings.
source: Several recent publications have highlighted a role for MFs, particularly M2 cells, in promoting regeneration of β cells in diverse experimental settings (Brissova et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2014), a function foretold by the reduced β-cell mass in MF-deficient Csf1op/op mice reported a decade ago (Banaei-Bouchareb et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brissova et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2014; Banaei-Bouchareb et al., 2004.

claim: Increased β-cell proliferation could result from up-regulation of the genes encoding Neurod1.
source: Increased β-cell proliferation could result from up-regulation of the genes encoding Neurod1 (Kojima et al., 2003), GLP-1R (De Leon et al., 2003), or various of the Reg family members (Unno et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2008), the latter perhaps a consequence of higher IL-22R expression (Hill et al., 2013) (see Figure 6B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kojima et al., 2003 and data in Figure 6B.

claim: Increased β-cell proliferation could result from up-regulation of the genes encoding GLP-1R.
source: Increased β-cell proliferation could result from up-regulation of the genes encoding Neurod1 (Kojima et al., 2003), GLP-1R (De Leon et al., 2003), or various of the Reg family members (Unno et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2008), the latter perhaps a consequence of higher IL-22R expression (Hill et al., 2013) (see Figure 6B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to De Leon et al., 2003 and data in Figure 6B.

claim: Increased β-cell proliferation could result from up-regulation of various Reg family members.
source: Increased β-cell proliferation could result from up-regulation of the genes encoding Neurod1 (Kojima et al., 2003), GLP-1R (De Leon et al., 2003), or various of the Reg family members (Unno et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2008), the latter perhaps a consequence of higher IL-22R expression (Hill et al., 2013) (see Figure 6B and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Unno et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2013 and data in Figure 6B.

claim: Protection of β-cells from apoptosis is likely to be an important outcome of inhibiting the NF-κB pathway.
source: Protection of β-cells from apoptosis is likely to be an important outcome of inhibiting the NF-κB pathway (Takahashi et al., 2010), but could also issue from enhanced expression of other known pro-survival factors, such as Cntfr (Rezende et al., 2007) and Tox3 (Dittmer et al., 2011) (see Figures 4 and 6B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takahashi et al., 2010; Rezende et al., 2007; Dittmer et al., 2011 and data in Figures 4 and 6B.

claim: β-cell differentiation and function should be fostered by up-regulation of genes encoding transcription factors such as Neurod1, Pdx1, Pax6, Nkx6-1 and Nkx2-2.
source: Lastly, β-cell differentiation and function should be fostered by up-regulation of genes encoding transcription factors such as Neurod1, Pdx1, Pax6, Nkx6-1 and Nkx2-2.
evidence: This is an inference based on known functions of these transcription factors and their up-regulation shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The significant delay in re-onset of diabetes in I-BET151-treated diabetic mice suggests functionally relevant improvement in β-cell function.
source: The significant delay in re-onset of diabetes in I-BET151-treated diabetic mice suggests functionally relevant improvement in β-cell function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Brd4 is an important element of so-called 'super-enhancers'.
source: First: Brd4 is an important element of so-called 'super-enhancers', defined as unusually long transcriptional enhancers that host an exceptionally high density of TFs—both cell-type-specific and general factors, including RNA polymerase-II, Mediator, p300 and Brd4 (Hnisz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hnisz et al., 2013.

claim: Super-enhancers are preferentially associated with loci that define and control the biology of particular cell-types, notably developmentally regulated and inducible genes.
source: Super-enhancers are preferentially associated with loci that define and control the biology of particular cell-types, notably developmentally regulated and inducible genes; intriguingly, disease-associated, including T1D-associated, nucleotide polymorphisms are especially enriched in the super-enhancers of disease-relevant cell-types (Hnisz et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hnisz et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2013.

claim: Disease-associated, including T1D-associated, nucleotide polymorphisms are especially enriched in the super-enhancers of disease-relevant cell-types.
source: Super-enhancers are preferentially associated with loci that define and control the biology of particular cell-types, notably developmentally regulated and inducible genes; intriguingly, disease-associated, including T1D-associated, nucleotide polymorphisms are especially enriched in the super-enhancers of disease-relevant cell-types (Hnisz et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hnisz et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2013.

claim: Genes associated with super-enhancers show unusually high sensitivity to BET-protein inhibitors.
source: Genes associated with super-enhancers show unusually high sensitivity to BET-protein inhibitors (Chapuy et al., 2013; Loven et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chapuy et al., 2013; Loven et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013.

claim: The bromodomain of Brd4 binds to acetyl-lysine residues on histone-4.
source: Second: although the bromodomain of Brd4 binds to acetyl-lysine residues on histone-4, and I-BET151 was modeled to inhibit this interaction, it is now known to bind to a few non-histone chromosomal proteins as well, notably NF-κB, a liaison also blocked by BET-protein inhibitors (Huang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Brd4 function.

claim: Brd4 is now known to bind to a few non-histone chromosomal proteins as well, notably NF-κB.
source: Second: although the bromodomain of Brd4 binds to acetyl-lysine residues on histone-4, and I-BET151 was modeled to inhibit this interaction, it is now known to bind to a few non-histone chromosomal proteins as well, notably NF-κB, a liaison also blocked by BET-protein inhibitors (Huang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014.

claim: The Brd4:NF-κB liaison is blocked by BET-protein inhibitors.
source: Second: although the bromodomain of Brd4 binds to acetyl-lysine residues on histone-4, and I-BET151 was modeled to inhibit this interaction, it is now known to bind to a few non-histone chromosomal proteins as well, notably NF-κB, a liaison also blocked by BET-protein inhibitors (Huang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012; Zou et al., 2014.

claim: The two bromodomains of Brd4 cooperatively recognize RelA acetylated at the K310 position.
source: The two bromodomains of Brd4 cooperatively recognize RelA acetylated at the K310 position, and this interaction is blocked by drugs like I-BET151 and JQ1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Brd4:NF-κB interaction.

claim: The Brd4:RelA interaction is blocked by drugs like I-BET151 and JQ1.
source: The two bromodomains of Brd4 cooperatively recognize RelA acetylated at the K310 position, and this interaction is blocked by drugs like I-BET151 and JQ1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about BET inhibitor mechanism.

claim: The HDAC inhibitor vorinostat was reported to inhibit T1D by a seemingly different mechanism impacting a multiplicity of cell-types.
source: Recently, another drug from the cancer world, the HDAC inhibitor, vorinostat, was reported to inhibit T1D, by a seemingly different mechanism impacting a multiplicity of cell-types (Christensen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Christensen et al., 2014.

claim: Epigenetic modulators would seem to be exciting candidates to explore in human T1D patients.
source: Thus, epigenetic modulators would seem to be exciting candidates to explore in human T1D patients.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The NF-κB pathway has been implicated in the death of β-cells associated with T1D, mainly the branches downstream of inflammatory cytokine and stress stimuli.
source: The NF-κB pathway has been implicated in the death of β-cells associated with T1D, mainly the branches downstream of inflammatory cytokine and stress stimuli (Cardozo et al., 2001; Cnop et al., 2005; Eldor et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cardozo et al., 2001; Cnop et al., 2005; Eldor et al., 2006.

claim: Several NF-κB-dependent transcripts previously reported to be induced in β cells by the inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IFN-γ were suppressed by I-BET151.
source: Several NF-κB-dependent transcripts previously reported to be induced in β cells by the inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IFN-γ (Cardozo et al., 2001) were suppressed by I-BET151, for example, Icam1, 1.45-fold; Traf2, 1.28-fold; Fabp5, 1.23-fold.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cardozo et al., 2001 and transcriptome data.

claim: I-BET151 appeared to have a positive impact on β-cell regeneration and/or function.
source: Overall, then, I-BET151 appeared to have a positive impact on β-cell regeneration and/or function.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the β-cell transcriptome and proliferation data.

claim: It has been reported that T cells in the immune infiltrate can induce β-cell replication.
source: Since it has been reported that T cells in the immune infiltrate can induce β-cell replication (Sreenan et al., 1999; Sherry et al., 2006; Dirice et al., 2013), we repeated the preceding experiments on Rag1-deficient NOD mice in order to address the possibility of a secondary effect mediated through lymphocytes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sreenan et al., 1999; Sherry et al., 2006; Dirice et al., 2013.
